name: Right atrium
func: The upper right chamber of the heart. It collects oxygen-poor blood returning from the body through the venae cavae and passes it to the right ventricle. It also holds the SA node, the heart's natural pacemaker.

levels.kid:
The **right atrium** is the **front door** of your heart. It is the room at the top right.

After blood has traveled all around your body, delivering oxygen, it comes home tired and needing more. Two big tubes bring that blood into the right atrium.

Then the right atrium gives a little squeeze and pushes the blood down through a door (a valve) into the room below it.

The right atrium also has a tiny, very important spot called the **pacemaker**. It sends out a little electric "tick" that tells your whole heart when to beat, over and over, all day long.
levels.hs:
The **right atrium** is the upper right chamber of the heart. It forms the heart's **right border** on a chest X-ray and lies in front of and to the right of the **left atrium**, separated from it by the **interatrial septum**. Below it is the **right ventricle**, and the two connect through the **tricuspid valve**. The ear-shaped flap sticking out from its front, the **right auricle** (atrial appendage), overlaps the root of the **aorta**.

Three main veins empty into it:
- The **superior vena cava (SVC)**, bringing blood from the head, neck and arms.
- The **inferior vena cava (IVC)**, bringing blood from the abdomen and legs.
- The **coronary sinus**, bringing used blood from the heart muscle itself.

The right atrium holds blood during the time the ventricle is contracting, then lets it flow into the right ventricle when the tricuspid valve opens. A final "**atrial kick**" squeezes in the last bit of blood.

In its wall, near where the SVC enters, sits the **sinoatrial (SA) node**, the heart's natural **pacemaker**. The **atrioventricular (AV) node** sits in its lower wall near the septum.

On the septum is an oval dip, the **fossa ovalis**, the remains of a hole that let blood skip the lungs before birth.
levels.college:
The right atrium has two developmentally distinct parts, separated on the inside by a muscular ridge, the **crista terminalis**, which corresponds to the **sulcus terminalis** on the outside:
- The **sinus venarum**, smooth-walled and posterior, derived from the embryonic **sinus venosus**. The SVC, IVC and coronary sinus open into it.
- The **atrium proper** and **auricle**, in front, lined with parallel muscle ridges called **pectinate muscles**, derived from the primitive atrium.

**Valves of the openings**: the IVC opening has a rudimentary **Eustachian valve**, which in the fetus directed oxygen-rich IVC blood toward the foramen ovale; the coronary sinus has the **Thebesian valve**.

The **fossa ovalis** is surrounded by a raised rim, the **limbus**. Before birth, the **foramen ovale** let blood pass from right to left atrium. At birth, rising left atrial pressure pushes the flap (septum primum) against the septum secundum, closing it. In about **25%** of adults the seal is incomplete: a **patent foramen ovale (PFO)**.

**Triangle of Koch**: bounded by the **tendon of Todaro**, the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve and the coronary sinus opening. The **AV node** sits at its apex; surgeons avoid this area to prevent heart block.

**SA node**: a crescent-shaped structure in the sulcus terminalis near the SVC, supplied by the **sinoatrial nodal artery**, which arises from the **RCA** in about 60% of people and the circumflex in the rest.

The atrial walls also release **atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)** when stretched, prompting the kidneys to excrete sodium and water.
levels.phd:
**SA node cells** lack a stable resting potential. Their spontaneous diastolic depolarization arises from the coupled **membrane clock** (**HCN4**-mediated funny current, T-type and L-type calcium currents, and declining delayed rectifier potassium currents) and **calcium clock** (local calcium releases from ryanodine receptors driving forward-mode **NCX1**). The node is a heterogeneous tissue: high-resolution optical mapping (Fedorov, Efimov) shows multiple leading pacemaker sites and specialized **sinoatrial conduction pathways** that insulate the node from hyperpolarizing atrial muscle, explaining how a small node can drive a large atrium.

The **transcription factor** network that builds the SA node includes **TBX3**, **SHOX2** and **ISL1**, which suppress the working atrial program (NKX2-5, connexin-40, connexin-43). Pacemaker cells are coupled by low-conductance **connexin-45** gap junctions. Reprogramming working myocytes with **TBX18** has created "biological pacemakers" in animal models.

**Atrial natriuretic peptide** is stored in atrial granules and released by stretch; it binds **NPR-A**, a guanylyl cyclase receptor, raising cGMP to cause vasodilation and natriuresis and to oppose the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

The right atrium's **sinus venosus** origin explains its smooth posterior wall and the location of the SA node, derived from the right sinus horn. **Atrial flutter** typically uses a macro-reentrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus, with the **cavotricuspid isthmus** (between the IVC and tricuspid valve) as the critical slow-conduction zone. The crista terminalis acts as a line of conduction block forming the posterior boundary. This anatomical understanding made catheter ablation of typical flutter highly successful.

Atrial stretch receptors (type A and B) send signals via the vagus, contributing to the **Bainbridge reflex**, a rise in heart rate with increased venous return.
levels.expert:
**Jugular venous pressure (JVP)**: the internal jugular vein acts as a manometer for right atrial pressure. A raised JVP suggests right heart failure, fluid overload, **tamponade** or **constrictive pericarditis** (with **Kussmaul sign**: JVP rising on inspiration). The **a wave** (atrial contraction) disappears in atrial fibrillation; large **cannon a waves** occur when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, as in complete heart block. **Giant v waves** suggest tricuspid regurgitation.

**Right atrial enlargement** on the ECG shows tall P waves in lead II (**P pulmonale**), often from lung disease or pulmonary hypertension.

**Arrhythmias**: **sick sinus syndrome** (SA node dysfunction causing slow rates or pauses) may need a **pacemaker**, whose right atrial lead is usually fixed in the auricle. **Typical atrial flutter** produces sawtooth flutter waves and is cured in most cases by **cavotricuspid isthmus ablation**.

**Atrial septal defects** (most commonly **secundum** type) cause right heart volume overload and a fixed split S2; many are closed with catheter-delivered devices. A **PFO** can allow **paradoxical embolism**, where a venous clot crosses into the systemic circulation and causes a **stroke**, especially in younger patients. A **bubble contrast echo** shows the shunt, and PFO closure reduces recurrent stroke risk in selected patients.

**Central venous catheters** are positioned with their tip at the junction of the **SVC and right atrium**. In neurosurgery, patients operated on in the sitting position risk **venous air embolism**; a multi-orifice catheter in the right atrium can aspirate air, and a PFO raises the danger of air crossing to the brain. **Right atrial myxoma** is rare compared with left.

keyPoints: Upper right chamber; forms the right heart border; tricuspid valve leads to the right ventricle
Receives the SVC, IVC and coronary sinus
Crista terminalis separates the smooth sinus venarum from the pectinate muscle area
Holds the SA node (pacemaker) and the AV node (triangle of Koch)
Fossa ovalis: incomplete closure = PFO, a route for paradoxical embolism

test.q: Which vessel does NOT empty into the right atrium?
test.explain: The pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium.

test.q: The oval dip in the interatrial septum left over from the fetal foramen ovale is the fossa ______.
test.explain: The fossa ovalis marks where the foramen ovale was; in about 25% of adults it remains patent.

test.q: The AV node lies at the apex of the triangle of:
test.explain: Koch's triangle: tendon of Todaro, septal tricuspid leaflet and coronary sinus opening.

test.q: Cannon a waves in the neck veins suggest:
test.explain: The atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve when atria and ventricles beat independently.

test.q: The muscular ridge inside the right atrium that separates its smooth and rough parts is the crista ______.
test.explain: It marks the boundary between the sinus venarum and the pectinate-muscle atrium.
